mappings.note: Converts units and computes the time for a 360 km run at 25 m/s: a speed calculation, which LO-104 names explicitly.
Finds the speed in two units and then the distance covered in four hours: several calculations on the same journey.
Compares 18 m/s with 72 km/h, which turns on converting one into the other. The work is arithmetic, so LO-104 rather than a classification outcome.

Distinguishes uniform from non-uniform motion through the highway and city-traffic examples. LO-98 and LO-99 cover materials and organisms, so a distinction between kinds of motion belongs with explaining the phenomenon.
Builds and calibrates a water clock from bottles and marks: a working device made from everyday materials, which is LO-107.
Times ten oscillations and divides by ten to get the period, which LO-104 names as the time period of a simple pendulum.
The smallest interval a wall clock can show is its least count, a question about how finely time can be measured.
Computes the speed of four or five trains from distance and time and then compares them: repeated speed calculation from collected data.
Calculates a speed in metres per second and converts it to kilometres per hour.
Two runners over the same distance, with the difference in their speeds worked out numerically.
Fills the gaps in a distance-time table by using the constant eight metres per ten seconds. Not LO-106, because the data stay in a table and no graph is plotted or read.
Judges the motion non-uniform and then computes the average speed over three hours; the calculation is what the marks rest on.
One-mark version of the two-runner comparison, decided by whoever takes less time over the same distance.
Time for the train journey in hours, a unit-conversion and division problem.
Speed from 180 km in three hours, the simplest speed calculation in the batch.
Horse against train once both speeds are in the same unit: again a conversion and comparison.
Reads equal distances in equal times as uniform motion, which is naming the kind of motion rather than computing anything.
Needs the average speed over three unequal hourly distances as well as the verdict, so the calculation dominates.
Which kind of motion we actually meet in daily life: the concept checked against everyday experience. Not LO-102, because no definition is being given.
Sunrise, the phases of the Moon and the seasons as the repeating events timekeeping was built on: the basis of the process explained.
Names the sundial from the fact that it uses a moving shadow: a device identified by how it looks and works.
Sand as what flows in an hourglass, another device identified by its working part.
The Ghatika-yantra as Aryabhata described it is a piece of the history of Indian science, so the appreciate-the-story outcome rather than plain device identification.
The outflow clock loses accuracy because the flow slows as the level drops: a defect traced to its cause.
Asks for three examples from the student's own experience to show non-uniform motion is the common case: the concept applied to daily life.
Checks eleven readings for equal distances in equal times and then computes the average speed over the whole run.
A three-stage journey where the speed needed for the last leg and the average speed overall must both be worked out: the heaviest calculation in the batch.
Names the time period as the time for one oscillation, the quantity LO-104 names for the simple pendulum.
Divides twenty seconds by ten oscillations to get the period: the pendulum calculation itself.
The period depends on length rather than mass or amplitude, which ties the measured quantity to the variable that governs it. Not LO-104, because nothing is calculated.
Two bobs of different mass on equal strings keep the same period, the same dependence tested from the negative side.
Quartz clocks work from the steady vibration of a crystal: how a modern clock keeps time, so the process outcome rather than device identification.
The second as the SI unit of time, the unit every measurement in this chapter is expressed in.
Sixty seconds in a minute: a conversion fact used in the chapter's calculations.
Sixty minutes in an hour, the companion conversion fact.
The speedometer as the instrument that reads speed: measurement of the quantity LO-104 names. Not LO-97, because what the instrument measures, not what it looks like, is the point.
The odometer as the instrument that totals distance travelled, the companion measuring instrument.
Defines uniform linear motion as a straight path at constant speed.
Equal distances in equal intervals as the defining test for uniform motion, the same definition in fill-in form.
Defines non-uniform linear motion as a straight path with changing speed, the counterpart definition.
